blocks.text: **Sperling (1960)** asked whether people report so few letters from a quick flash because they only register a few, or because the image fades before they can say them all. He flashed arrays of three rows of four letters and compared three report methods: **whole report** (name as many as you can), **partial report** (a tone right after the display cues one row) and **delayed partial report** (the tone comes after a delay).
children: The question was whether the reporting limit reflects storage or fading.

blocks.text: In whole report people named about **4.5 of 12 letters**, roughly a third. In immediate partial report they named about **3.3 of 4 letters (82 percent)** of the cued row, for any row. Because the tone came only after the display was gone and nobody knew which row would be cued, information about all rows must have been available at first. With a delayed tone, performance fell to about one letter, and by about **1 second** it was near the whole-report level.

So **sensory memory has a large capacity but fast decay**. The trap is reading the whole-report score of four or five items as the size of the store, when it is a limit on reporting before the trace fades.
children: Whole report measures reporting speed against fading, not capacity.

blocks.text: **Brown (1958)** and **Peterson and Peterson (1959)** asked how fast short-term memory fades when rehearsal is blocked. Participants saw three letters, counted backward by threes during a delay of 3 to 18 seconds, and then recalled the letters. The counting prevented ordinary maintenance rehearsal, and the researchers also tracked where each trial fell in the series.

On the **first trial** recall stayed high even after 18 seconds. By the **third trial** recall at 18 seconds was lower, and after many trials it fell to almost nothing. The same delay did far more damage when more earlier letters had piled up.
children: Trial history, not only elapsed time, drove the forgetting.

blocks.text: This is **proactive interference**: earlier trigrams made the new one harder to keep. The trap is the average over all trials, which looks like steady decay with time but mixes easy early trials with hard late ones. The steep drop comes mostly from the later trials, so the pattern is evidence for interference as well as decay.

**Alvarez and Cavanagh (2004)** asked whether visual short-term memory capacity is set by the number of items or by the amount of information in them. They used **change detection**: people viewed a first array (S1) for 100 milliseconds, then judged whether a second display (S2), shown for 2,000 milliseconds, was the same or different. They varied the number of colored squares, what changed in colored bars (angle, color or both), and the complexity of the objects (colored squares, Chinese characters, random polygons, shaded cubes).

Accuracy fell dramatically above about **four items**. Remembering two features of a bar was about as easy as remembering one. Capacity also fell as objects became more complex, from about four for colored squares to fewer than two for shaded cubes.
children: Capacity depends on how much information each object carries.

blocks.text: So visual short-term memory holds about **three to four whole objects**. The trap is carrying over Miller's seven: for visual memory the estimate is about four, and fewer for complex objects.

Can chunking and knowledge let people hold far more in short-term memory? **Ericsson and colleagues (1980)** trained a college student on digit span. By organizing the digits into familiar running times, he reached a span of about **79 digits**.

**Chase and Simon (1973)** tested player skill (masters versus beginners) and board type (real-game arrangement versus random arrangement) by measuring how many chess pieces people placed correctly after a brief look. Masters placed far more pieces than beginners on real-game boards, but they were no better on random boards.
children: The masters' edge vanished when the familiar patterns were removed.

blocks.text: Both results show that **chunking with knowledge from long-term memory** stretches effective capacity. Experts do not have bigger short-term memories. The trap is crediting the masters with a larger store, when it is their knowledge of real patterns that helps.

title: Conrad · sound-based errors after visual presentation

blocks.text: **Conrad (1964)** asked whether errors in remembering seen letters are based on how the letters look or how they sound. He flashed letters briefly, half the time similar and half the time not similar, and participants wrote them down.

Errors more often swapped in a letter that **sounded like** the target (B for E) than one that **looked like** it (F for E). The letters entered through vision, but the confusions followed their spoken names.
children: This is the phonological similarity effect.

blocks.text: So seen letters are recoded into a **sound-based form** in working memory, through the phonological loop. The trap is treating presentation format as memory code: what people see is not the same as the form in which it is maintained.

title: Word length, bilingual digit span, and articulatory suppression

blocks.text: What limits how much verbal material the **phonological loop** can hold? **Baddeley and colleagues (1975, 1984)** found that people remembered more short words than long words, because long words take longer to pronounce and rehearse. **Ellis and Hennelly (1980)** tested Welsh-English bilingual children and found a shorter digit span in Welsh than in English, because Welsh number names take longer to say.
The Welsh-English gap comes from **pronunciation time**, not from the values of the numbers. Verbal span depends on how much can be rehearsed in about **1.5 to 2 seconds**.
children: Faster rehearsal keeps more items active.

blocks.text: **Articulatory suppression**, speaking while memorizing, occupies the rehearsal process. It lowered recall and reduced both the word-length effect and the phonological similarity effect, which shows that speech-based rehearsal is used to maintain verbal information.

title: Brooks · sentence and F dual-task comparisons

blocks.text: **Brooks (1968)** asked whether a response interferes more when it uses the same kind of memory as the thing being held. He varied the response mode, speaking or pointing, across two memory tasks. In one, people memorized a sentence and judged whether each word was a noun. In the other, they memorized an F and judged whether each corner was an inside or outside corner.

With the **sentence**, pointing was easier than speaking, because holding the sentence used the phonological loop and speaking competed with it. With the **F**, speaking was easier than pointing, because holding the F used the visuospatial sketchpad and pointing added a spatial demand.
children: Interference depends on the combination of tasks.

blocks.text: The results reverse, so neither speaking nor pointing is easier overall. The pattern supports some independence between verbal and visual or spatial memory.

title: Shepard and Metzler · angle and mental-rotation time

blocks.text: Do people mentally rotate objects, and does more rotation take more time? **Shepard and Metzler (1971)** showed pairs of block-built objects at different orientations and measured the reaction time to judge whether the two objects matched. The rotation could be in the picture plane or in depth.
For picture-plane pairs, reaction time **increased as the angle increased**, approximately linearly. A larger angle needs a larger mental transformation before the objects can be compared.
children: This points to an active operation on a spatial representation, not storage of an unchanged picture.

blocks.text: The trap is mixing up the two kinds of turning: picture-plane rotation turns within the flat plane, while depth rotation turns in three-dimensional space.

title: Vogel · relevant load, distractors, and filtering efficiency

blocks.text: Do people with higher working-memory capacity keep irrelevant items out better? **Vogel and colleagues (2005)** first measured capacity to separate higher- and lower-capacity participants. They then recorded an event-related potential (ERP), a memory-related brain response, during a 900 millisecond retention interval, while people judged whether a relevant orientation had changed. Displays had two relevant red bars, four relevant red bars, or two red bars plus two irrelevant blue bars.

High-capacity people showed a larger response for four items than for two, and **little change** when blue distractors were added. For low-capacity people, adding distractors raised the response toward the four-item level, so irrelevant material entered working memory. Capacity correlated **positively** with filtering efficiency.
children: Better filtering goes with higher capacity.

blocks.text: So capacity depends on which items get in as well as how many targets there are. The trap is the direction of the signal: a bigger response means a stronger negative deflection, not a more positive voltage.
